newsitem.title: GERMANY: German ex-communists vote to help oust Kohl.
newsitem.headline: German ex-communists vote to help oust Kohl.

text.p: Germany's ex-communists have voted at their annual congress in favour of teaming up with other opposition parties to help them oust Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government after the next general election.

Delegates at the Party of Democratic Socialism's (PDS) conference in the northeastern city of Schwerin approved a motion on Friday evening saying the party could "make a direct contribution" to removing Kohl's centre-right coalition.

"The important thing is to make real changes in society and we won't manage those alone," said PDS parliamentary leader Gregor Gysi, whose charisma and telegenic personality have made him the party's highest profile official.

The motion, approved by a large majority of delegates, was a victory for reformers in the successor party to the hardline communists who ruled East Germany. Marxist members had wanted the party to remain strictly an opposition group.

"If we put forward a programme and then have the chance to convert parts of it into reality but say no, won't do it for ideological reasons...that's how you make a laughing stock out of yourself in politics," Gysi told German Radio.

The motion left open whether the PDS would be willing to form a coalition with Germany's two main opposition parties, the Social Democrats (SPD) and the Greens, after the 1998 elections or if it would merely offer tacit support.

Gysi said because the motion's success had shown the party was on the right track, he would not stand for re-election to the party's leadership committee and could now concentrate on his role as parliamentary chief.
Gysi appeared unconcerned by the stance of the SPD and the Greens, who have said they could not join forces with the PDS until it distances itself more clearly from its past.
"The decisions of the SPD and the Greens have a sell-by date and that sell-by date is the elections," Gysi said.
Opninion polls give the PDS between four and six percent support nationally but around 20 percent in eastern Germany.
The party has styled itself as the champion of east Germans who feel let down by the mainstream Bonn parties during the painful change from communism to capitalism.
